t: The Secretary of the Army may establish or develop installations and facilities by proceeding with construction made necessary by changes in missions and responsibilities which have been occasioned by (1) unforeseen security considerations, (2) new weapons developments, (3) new and unforeseen research and development requirements, (4) improved production schedules, or (5) revisions in the tasks or functions assigned to a military installation or facility or for environmental considerations, if the Secretary of Defense determines that deferral of such construction for inclusion in the next Military Construction Authorization Act would be inconsistent with interests of national security and, in connection therewith, may acquire, construct, convert, rehabilitate, or install permanent or temporary public works, including land acquisition, site preparation, appurtenances, utilities, and equipment in the total amount of $20,000,000. The Secretary of the Army, or the Secretary’s designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section, including those real estate actions pertaining thereto. This authorization shall expire on October 1, 1981, or on the date of the enactment of the Military Construction Authorization Act for fiscal year 1982, whichever is later, except for those public works projects concerning which the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives have been notified pursuant to this section prior to such date.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the notification requirement and the Secretary of Defense's determination are procedural participation steps. But the only actors are the Secretary of the Army, the Secretary of Defense, and congressional committees, all of whom are inside the federal government, and the notice comes after a final decision. No state, local, public, expert, or other outside party is consulted or given a right to object or sue.
fable.s: shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Secretary of the Army to notify congressional committees after a decision has been made. Congress is considered part of the federal government, and notification to Congress is explicitly excluded from the definition of participation. There is no requirement to consult with or coordinate with outside parties (such as the public, states, or private entities) before making the decision.
qwen_block.s: The Secretary of the Army, or the Secretary’s designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section

opus.w: The only formal interaction is a notice to the congressional Armed Services Committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. The other actors are also federal: the Secretary of the Army, the Secretary of Defense and any designee. No outside party is consulted, and the section creates no hearing, comment period, rulemaking or right to sue, so it does not cross the federal boundary.
opus.s: The Secretary of the Army, or the Secretary’s designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section
opus.b:
**Tempting but wrong reading:** The section requires the Secretary of the Army to "notify the Committees on Armed Services," and expiration depends on whether those committees were notified. That looks like a formal outside check on the decision. It doesn't count, because Congress and its committees are inside the federal government.

Everyone else involved is federal too: the Secretary of the Army, the Secretary of Defense and any designee. No state, tribe, expert, company or member of the public is consulted, and there is no hearing, comment period, rulemaking or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary of the Army to notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives. According to the definition, Congress and its committees are inside the federal government. Notification to internal government bodies does not constitute participation with outside parties.
qwen_chat.s: The Secretary of the Army, or the Secretary’s designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that notifying the Committees on Armed Services constitutes "participation" because it involves informing outside entities before or during a decision. However, the definition explicitly states that "Congress, its committees and members... are all INSIDE the federal government." Therefore, reporting to Congress is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties.
